Built to Last

Josh and Jennifer Johnson are carrying forward a distinctive American sawmill, improving it where it matters, and building the business around the life they deliberately chose.

Business
Brand X Sawmills LLC
Location
White Sulphur Springs area, Montana
Product
90-degree swing-frame sawmills
FBS
Six-Month Essentials program

Starting Again on Purpose

By the time Josh and Jennifer Johnson were ready to restart production at Brand X Sawmills in 2026, they had already done something many business owners find almost impossible: they had stopped.

Production had been paused for roughly a year while they moved from Lewistown to the White Sulphur Springs area, built a new home and shop, and reorganized the business around the place where they intend to stay. That pause was not a retreat from Brand X. It was part of a longer plan.

In one Forest Business School session near the end of the move, Jennifer was working on Brand X social media while Josh was back in the shop replenishing what he calls the “blue bins” — the small parts, welding fixtures, and components that make final assembly possible. The scene was a good snapshot of the partnership. Jennifer was rebuilding the outward-facing side of the business while Josh rebuilt the physical flow of production.

The Johnsons are not trying to create the biggest sawmill company in America. They are trying to build a durable one, with a product they believe in, customers they can serve personally, and enough control over the business to support the life they want.

“We’re essentialists here with our lifestyle and our business.”

Josh Johnson, FBS Essentials

A Mill Worth Taking On

Brand X did not begin with Josh and Jennifer. The sawmill was designed by Jay Brand in Condon, Montana, in 2004 after decades of experience with other mills. Brand built more than 200 Brand X sawmills before his death in 2016. Years later, during the COVID era, the opportunity arose for the Johnsons — longtime friends of the Brand family — to carry the business forward.

They did not say yes immediately. They studied the opportunity and asked whether it really fit them. What finally settled the question was seeing the mill work.

“Our jaws hit the floor. We were like, this thing is so cool. It’s so precise. It makes boards so quickly.”

Jennifer Johnson, recalling the first time she saw a Brand X mill run

Once they understood what the machine could do, she said, “We have to do this.”

The enthusiasm makes sense when the machine is seen in operation. The Brand X is a 90-degree swing-frame sawmill: its circular blade cuts horizontally and vertically, and it cuts in both directions of travel. Dimensional lumber can be produced without repeatedly turning the log. The company builds the machines in Montana, fully assembled, and the Johnsons say Brand X is the only swing-frame sawmill currently manufactured in the United States. They also try to source as many components domestically as practical.

How the swing frame works

Because the blade swings through 90 degrees and cuts in both directions of travel, dimensional lumber comes off the mill without repeatedly turning the log.

The basic idea is deliberately mechanical and straightforward. Brand X describes the mill as easy to use, without unnecessary gadgets, and that simplicity has become part of the Johnsons’ own product philosophy.

But carrying forward Jay Brand’s design has not meant freezing it in time.

Early after taking over the business, Josh noticed a pattern in replacement-parts sales. One costly component failed repeatedly, and when it failed it often damaged surrounding parts. A less thoughtful business might have accepted those replacements as recurring revenue. Josh went the other way.

“Instead of producing attachments and growing the business in a different direction, I really focused on figuring out what this failure consisted of and how to eliminate it.”

Josh Johnson

He redesigned the system, developed an updated replacement kit, and stopped making the old part.

That small story says a great deal about Brand X under the Johnsons. Product improvement is not defined by adding features. Sometimes improvement means removing a failure permanently.

Two Different Skill Sets, One Business

Josh’s route to sawmill manufacturing came through machinery. He spent years as a mechanic at a New Holland dealership, later operated an independent repair business, and has more than two decades of experience across fabrication, welding, diesel and small-engine repair, and hydraulics. At Brand X he is the lead fabricator, mechanic, and product developer.

Jennifer came from a different direction. Her background includes education and newspaper reporting, along with extensive customer-service experience. At Brand X she handles much of the bookkeeping, invoicing, correspondence, website and social-media work, and the organizational work that turns fabricated machines into a functioning business.

The division is not absolute — Josh spends substantial time talking with technically serious customers, and Jennifer is deeply involved in product and business decisions — but both understand the value of comparative advantage.

“I’m a fabricator,” Josh said during a discussion of specific knowledge. “I don’t do the things that even my wife does in this business. I stay in my own lane and I do the things I’m best at because that’s where I’m going to be productive.”

That combination matters to customers. Brand X is small enough that the person explaining the machine may be one of the people who built it. The Johnsons meet customers, orient them to safe operation and maintenance, and remain available afterward.

“If you have a question, you can call and get the guy who built it.”

Brand X Sawmills, on customer service

For a specialized machine sold to owner-operators, that is not a small point of differentiation. Brand X is not competing only on steel, horsepower, blade size, or price. It is also selling access to the people who know the machine intimately.

Discipline Before Growth

The Johnsons’ approach to money is similarly direct.

They spent seven years living in a camper as part of the process of staying out of debt and working toward the property and lifestyle they wanted. During an FBS discussion about status and spending, Jennifer contrasted their habits with the steady pressure to display success through new pickups, campers, and other visible purchases. Their approach, she said, is closer to “drive until the wheels fall off.”

By January 2026, when the Essentials group was discussing Profit First, the Johnsons could say that they had paid off the business completely about two years earlier.

“Brand X Sawmills has zero debt right now. We’re super excited about that. We don’t plan to get into that either.”

The Johnsons, to the FBS Essentials group

That does not mean refusing to invest. It means being clear about what an investment is supposed to accomplish.

The same discipline appears in production. Josh has developed a component-building sequence in which several weeks of shop work may produce no visible finished mill. Then final assembly begins and prepared components come off the shelf in order. It took several production cycles to refine that flow. By then, what can look from the outside like a small fabrication shop has become a system.

And it appears in product strategy. Josh has considered digital readouts and additional automation, but the question is not whether more technology is possible. The question is whether it improves the mill enough to justify greater cost and complexity for the customer.

The Forest Business School Fit

That is the point at which Josh and Jennifer’s experience intersects with the Forest Business School’s six-month Essentials program.

They did not enter Essentials because they needed to learn how to weld, repair machinery, talk with customers, or work hard. They already knew those things. The questions in front of them were the questions that arrive after a capable person has built a real business: What does the product actually cost to build as steel prices move? How much parts inventory is enough? Which improvements create value and which merely add complexity? How much demand is enough? How should profit, taxes, and cash reserves be structured? What does the business eventually need to provide for the owners, including long-term security and health insurance?

Those are management questions, and they do not solve themselves simply because someone is excellent at a trade.

Essentials is built around approximately six months of nearly weekly, one-hour evening video sessions. Participants work through assigned books, audiobooks, and podcasts and discuss the ideas with other people running businesses, managing operations, or working in forestry, logging, wood products, land management, and related fields. There are no grades, papers, or busywork. The expectation is that participants will think seriously, engage with their peers, and apply useful frameworks to their actual work.

That format fit the Johnsons particularly well. They already had a habit of reading together. During the program, Jennifer said she and Josh would often listen to an audiobook together, stop it, discuss what they had just heard, and then continue. Near the end of Essentials she admitted that she was “almost sad that the program is going to end” because she wanted to keep the habit going.

More important than enjoying the material, however, was what they did with it.

Learning That Reaches the Shop Floor

In their capstone discussion, Josh singled out the 80/20 principle as one of the most actionable ideas in the program. It was not always comfortable: prioritizing the vital few means admitting that some work, even work one has become accustomed to doing, is not equally valuable. But he found the framework useful for deciding where his time in the shop should go.

Jennifer highlighted Profit First. The method’s emphasis on separating money by purpose — including profit and taxes — arrived at an opportune time for a business that had already eliminated its debt and was preparing for a new operating chapter. Later, in a peer discussion about hiring, Jennifer remembered a Profit First suggestion: before hiring, set aside the would-be employee’s pay for a period and see whether the business can actually sustain it. A fellow participant immediately called it “a good reminder.”

Essentialism landed even more directly.

Josh said the book reinforced instincts the Johnsons already had. Together they described how it helped settle a product question they had been uncertain about: whether to develop a slabber for the Brand X mill.

After working through the material, their conclusion was simple: they had made the right decision not to go down that path. “We just need to keep it simple and be straightforward with what we offer.”

80/20

A way to decide where shop time actually goes — and to admit that familiar work is not automatically valuable work.

Profit First

Separating money by purpose, and testing a hire by setting the pay aside first to see whether the business can carry it.

Essentialism

The framework that settled an open product question by confirming what Brand X would not build.

This is an important distinction in how the Johnsons used FBS. The program did not hand them a business plan. Often it gave them a framework with which to test a decision they were already considering. Sometimes the result was to change direction. Sometimes it was to proceed with more confidence. And sometimes the best business decision was to decline an opportunity.

The peer group mattered, too. FBS participants brought different corners of the forest economy into the same conversation, and those relationships did not remain confined to a video screen.

One participant, forester Shavonne Sargent, later visited the Johnsons in Montana and operated a Brand X mill herself. Back with the group, she joked that now that she had run one and met Josh and Jennifer, she would “probably be a little bit of a pusher — not on commission.”

Other participants suggested referral channels, publications, forestry contacts, and ways to demonstrate the mill to the people most likely to appreciate it. For a niche manufacturer, those connections may be more useful than generic exposure.

The Right Seventeen Customers

Jennifer has seen the relationship between exposure and demand directly. During the program she explained that almost every time Brand X posts new material, inquiries begin arriving and she ends up preparing quotes. Yet the company can build only about 17 mills in a year.

“We don’t need a whole lot of business.”

Jennifer Johnson

That statement sounds almost heretical in an era when businesses are routinely told to maximize traffic, followers, leads, and scale. For Brand X, it is simply arithmetic.

The marketing problem is not how to make millions of people aware of a swing-frame sawmill. It is how to make Brand X visible and credible to the relatively small number of people each year for whom this particular machine is the right answer.

The goal isn’t maximum demand. It’s enough of the right demand.

That is why the current relaunch is interesting. Jennifer is thinking about name recognition and how to put Brand X back in front of the right people after a year away from production. Josh is thinking about parts inventory, steel prices, production flow, and what — if anything — should change in the machine.

Those are not separate problems. One side determines what the company promises; the other determines whether it can deliver that promise profitably.

Building the Business to Fit the Life

There is an easy way to tell a story like this badly: turn it into a tale of entrepreneurial sacrifice followed by inevitable success.

That is not the Johnsons’ story.

Brand X is still a small manufacturing company. Steel prices move. Parts have to be stocked before they are needed. Customers need support. Health insurance and long-term financial security do not become easy simply because the shop is on your own property. Relaunching after a production pause requires rebuilding attention without creating more demand than the operation can responsibly serve.

Josh and Jennifer are still working through those questions.

What makes their story useful is that they have become increasingly clear about the criteria by which they will answer them.

They want Brand X to remain a well-built, serviceable American-made machine. They want to improve weaknesses rather than add features for appearance’s sake. They want good customers and enough demand, not demand at any cost. They want the business financially sound. They want a production system that Josh can control and a customer relationship that does not disappear after the sale. And they want the company to support the rural life they spent years building toward.

Jennifer is also the partner inclined to ask what might go wrong before a decision is made. During an FBS discussion of pre-mortems and decision-making, she acknowledged that the habit can occasionally drive Josh crazy.

“However, I think it also keeps us from making a lot of mistakes.”

Jennifer Johnson

That may be as good a summary of the Johnson partnership as any. Josh is predisposed to understand how the machine works and how to make it work better. Jennifer is predisposed to think about what comes next, what the customer sees, what the books say, and where a decision might lead. Neither skill set is sufficient by itself.

Together, they are carrying forward a sawmill with a history, but they are not trying to recreate someone else’s company. They are building their version of Brand X: simpler where simplicity helps, improved where experience exposes a weakness, personal in its customer relationships, and deliberately limited by what two owners can do well.

For the Forest Business School, that is also the point of Essentials. The program is not designed to teach capable professionals their trade. It is designed for people who already have something real at stake and want better frameworks for deciding what to do with it.

Josh and Jennifer Johnson came with a real business, an unusual machine, a substantial amount of hard-earned experience, and some difficult questions.

They left with better ways to work on those questions — and a clearer sense that sometimes the most valuable answer in business is not what to add next, but what is essential enough to keep.

About the Forest Business School Essentials Program

The Forest Business School’s flagship Essentials program is a six-month program of professional development for mid-career working landscape professionals. It includes nearly weekly one-hour evening video sessions, rigorous reading and listening, Socratic peer discussion, and an expectation that participants apply what they learn in their actual businesses, agencies, and professional practices. There are no grades, papers, or busywork.

The program is free to accepted participants through partner funding; participants obtain their own reading or listening materials. Successful completers receive a certificate, and CFE credits are available through SAF.

Essentials is selective by design. It is intended for capable, self-motivated people in forestry, logging, wood products, land management, and related fields who are willing to engage honestly, consider new frameworks, and put useful ideas to work.
